explanation: Its cone-shaped eye turrets scan independently, then lock together on prey to judge distance before the sticky tongue shoots out. An owl cannot move its eyes at all and turns its head instead.

claims.text: Chameleons can move each eye independently, looking in different directions at the same time.
Owls, tarsiers and tree frogs cannot point their eyes in different directions independently.
Before striking, a chameleon focuses both eyes on its prey to judge distance.
Owls cannot move their eyes within their sockets and turn their heads instead.

evidence.restatement: Chameleons move each eye independently and can look in two directions at once.
Owl and tarsier eyes are fixed in their sockets, and tree frogs do not swivel their eyes independently in different directions.
Before a strike both eyes converge on the prey, and the chameleon gauges distance by focusing.
Owls' tubular eyes are essentially immobile, so owls turn their heads instead.
Chameleons can aim each eye independently, looking in two directions at once.
Owls have fixed tubular eyes, tarsiers turn the head instead, and tree frogs do not aim their eyes separately.
Before striking, a chameleon points both eyes at the prey and uses focus to judge the distance.
Owls cannot swivel their eyes in the sockets and turn the head instead.
